lede: Chronicle (Tamnan) · ตำนาน accounts for 1,060 catalogued manuscripts, 2 of them flagged research-priority. It clusters in Phrae (24% of the corpus for this genre), ahead of Chiang Mai and Phayao. Nearly all (94%) are written in Tham Lanna · อักษรธรรมล้านนา script. By support it leans to palm-leaf · ใบลาน (93%) over mulberry paper (saa) · กระดาษสา (4%). Dated witnesses run 1574–2024 CE (684 of 1,060 carry a date).

authored.title: Chronicle (Tamnan)
authored.body_html:
What this is

Tamnan (ตำนาน) is the northern chronicle, and at 1,060 witnesses it is the third-largest genre in this archive — behind only the canon and the jātaka. It is also the most narrative body of writing the north produced about itself. These are the stories the muang told to explain why the ground under them was holy: how a relic reached a particular hill, why a queen came up a particular river, which king the Buddha personally prophesied, and what happened to the city that ate the wrong fish.

Six hundred and seventeen of the 1,060 titles literally begin ตำนาน or ทำนาน — "the tamnan of." A hundred and seventy-six name a ธาตุ (that, a relic or the stupa holding it). A hundred and twenty-four name a เมือง (muang, a polity). Forty-seven carry วงส์ (vaṃsa, lineage). That distribution is the genre's whole argument in miniature: relic, place, descent. Everything else is commentary.

The form: history with the sacred as its engine

A tamnan is not a chronicle that happens to mention miracles. It is a chronicle in which the miracle is the causal mechanism. Ask a tamnan why a dynasty rules from a particular hill and it will not answer with a battle or a marriage. It will answer: because a relic came to rest there, and the relic chose.

This is worth stating plainly, because it is what makes the genre legible. In a tamnan the ordinary machinery of history — armies, succession, taxation — is present but demoted. It is the effect of the sacred fact, not the cause of it. The Buddha walks a valley and prophesies; centuries later a king who obeys the prophecy prospers and a king who ignores it does not. A relic is enshrined; the polity that houses it becomes legitimate, and the neighbouring polity that wants legitimacy has to acquire a relic of its own. Whole wars in these texts are, at bottom, arguments about custody of bone.

Inference — this is why the catalogue's own three-way split of the genre keeps leaking. The raw labels are Buddhist Chronicle (569), plain Tamnan (328), and Secular History (159) — but a genre built on sacred causation cannot cleanly yield a secular half. The "secular" shelf here holds the Pali Cāmadevīvaṃsa (ms 1350, Wat Sung Men, 1833), whose heroine is invited to found a city by a hermit; it holds eight copies of ปฐมมูลมูลี, a cosmogony; it holds seven of ปฐมกัป, the first aeon. Those are not secular documents. They are documents the cataloguer had nowhere else to put. The split is real as a labelling fact and soft as a content fact, and the three sub-pages take that up in detail.

The Buddha walked here

The master narrative of the Lanna tamnan is พระเจ้าเลียบโลก — Phra Chao Liap Lok, "the Buddha circuits the world." The collection holds 16 witnesses of it, copied at Wat Chiang Man in Chiang Mai (ms 776, 1834; ms 788; ms 792), at Wat Sung Men in Phrae (ms 2010, 1875), at Wat Na Pang in Nan (ms 638, 1815), at Wat Si Khom Kham in Phayao (ms 3511, 1933), at Wat Ban Laeo in Chiang Rai (ms 3510, 1919) — the same text recopied in seven provinces across a century and a half, which is what a foundational narrative looks like in a manuscript catalogue.

Tradition holds — the story is a walking tour. The Buddha, with Ānanda beside him, travels north out of the Ganges plain and up the valleys of what will become Lanna, and at each stop a local — a Lua hillman, a hunter, a farmer, in some tellings animals, a crow, a pair of mice — offers him something small and poor. He accepts it, smiles, and gives back a hair from his head, or presses a footprint into rock, or simply says: after my parinibbāna, a relic of mine will come to rest in this place, and there will be a great city here. The genre's entire premise is loaded into that sentence. Every relic-stupa in the north can then be read as the prophecy coming true on schedule, and every tamnan of a that is a receipt.

The corpus keeps the companion pieces too: 19 chronicle titles name a พระบาท (phra bat, the footprint), 12 a เกสาธาตุ (kesa dhātu, the hair-relic). Ms 780 at Wat Chiang Man (1812) is titled Tamnan pha cao wai pha bat pha that — the chronicle of the Buddha paying homage to footprint and relic — and ms 6794 at Wat Mae Wa Luang, Lampang, files ตำนานแม่ระมิงค์, the chronicle of the Ping river, explicitly as phuk 9 of the Liap Lok. The river gets its own fascicle of the Buddha's itinerary. That is how completely this text organises northern geography.

The relics that have chronicles

Because each that generated its own paperwork, the relic-tamnan double as a map. The atlas and the wat gazetteer can be read against this list:

  • พระธาตุดอยสุเทพ — Doi Suthep, 10 witnesses, and not one of them from Doi Suthep: ms 6046 was copied at Wat Phra That Hariphunchai in Lamphun in 1920, ms 3588 at Wat Mueang Mo in Phrae in 1884 (titled Tamnan pha mahacinathat cao sutep, the Victor's Relic on Suthep), ms 5985 at Wat Luang Ratchasanthan in Phayao in 1909. A famous relic's chronicle travels further than the relic does. Tradition holds — the famous version: a relic brought north by the monk Sumana splits in two at Wat Suan Dok; the second half is loaded onto a white elephant, which is turned loose, climbs the mountain, trumpets three times, circles three times, kneels, and dies on the spot — and there the stupa goes. Note who decides: not the king, the elephant. The mountain itself is named for a hermit, Wāsudeva, which is why the lersi are never far from a Lanna foundation story. See Wat Phra That Doi Suthep.
  • พระธาตุดอยตุง — Doi Tung, 13 witnesses, several tying it explicitly to the old capital: ms 2750 and ms 3586, both Tamnan that doi tung mueang ciang saen, copied at Wat Mueang Mo in 1884; ms 6849 at Wat Si Khom Kham in 1960. Tradition holds — the name is the ตุง, the banner: a flag of enormous length was raised on the summit and every acre its shadow crossed was given to the shrine. Land tenure decided by a shadow. See Wat Phra That Doi Tung.
  • พระธาตุหริภุญชัย — Lamphun, 17 witnesses under its several spellings (หริภุญ, ละพูร, ลพูน, รภุญ), including ms 3790 at Wat Duang Di, Chiang Mai (1861) and ms 6708 at Wat Chiang Man (1833). Tradition holds — the relic lay buried under the royal latrine until a king who learned of it moved his palace rather than the bone. See Wat Phra That Hariphunchai.
  • พระธาตุช่อแฮ — Phrae's own, 7 witnesses, all from Phrae temples, the earliest ms 6638 at Wat Phra Luang Sung Men dated 1780. A muang keeps its own relic's paperwork at home. See Wat Phra That Cho Hae.
  • พระธาตุแช่แห้ง — Nan, 5 witnesses, ms 782 copied at Wat Chiang Man in 1815 and ms 6767 at Wat Nong Bua, Nan, in 1883, the latter pairing Chae Haeng with Phu Phiang, the hill it stands on. See Wat Phra That Chae Haeng.
  • พระธาตุลำปางหลวง — and here the catalogue does something lovely. Ms 4912, held at Wat Phra That Lampang Luang itself and dated 1713, is titled จารึกตำนานมหาธาตุ — the inscription of the chronicle of the great relic: a palm-leaf copy of a stone inscription of a relic chronicle, kept at the relic. Three media deep, and it never left home.

Beyond bone, the genre chronicles images: 23 titles name the พระแก้ว, the crystal or emerald Buddha, and the cluster around วัดพระแก้วดอนเต้า at Lampang (ms 777, ms 2254, ms 3558, ms 3559, ms 6594, ms 6797 and more) keeps calling the city by its old name เมืองกุกุตะนคอร, Kukkuṭanagara — the rooster city, which is where the north's obsession with the kai touches its chronicles. See Wat Phra Kaeo Don Tao.

The queen who was sent for

The other great founding story in the collection has a woman at the centre of it. นางจามเทวี — Camadevi of Haripuñjaya — carries nine witnesses, and they scatter across all three sub-genre labels at once, which tells you how little the labels mean here. The Pali Cāmadevīvaṃsa (ms 1350) and Pali cammatewi (ms 1331) were both copied at Wat Sung Men, in 1833 and 1842, and both are filed Secular History; ms 201 at Wat Phra That Chang Kham, Nan (1869) and ms 4167, Tamnan mae cao mae cam tewi (1964), are filed Buddhist Chronicle; ms 6710 at Wat Pratu Pa, Lamphun (1928) and ms 6880 at Wat Mae Kham Nam Lat, Chiang Rai (1953) are plain Tamnan. One queen, three shelves, a hundred and thirty years of continuous recopying — the latest of them made when the Second World War was in living memory.

Tradition holds — a hermit builds a city in the Ping valley and finds he has no one to rule it, so he sends downriver to Lavo (Lopburi) for a princess. Camadevi comes north by boat, pregnant, at the head of a convoy carrying monks, scribes, physicians, sculptors and metalworkers — the story is quite specific that what founds a city is not an army but a staffed institution. She bears twin sons and splits the north between them. The tamnan is calmly clear that the ruler of the new polity is a woman, that she was recruited, and that her mandate came from an ascetic rather than a battlefield.

The founding stories keep the same shape at city scale: 27 titles name Chiang Mai, 33 name Chiang Saen. Ms 6593 is tāṃnān nabapurī mīöṅ biṅ jīeṅ hmaï1 — the tamnan of Nopburi, the muang of the Ping, Chiang Mai — the city under the ceremonial name Mangrai gave it. Where a tamnan narrates a founder it stands one step from the charter that legitimises him, which is why the Mangrai code and the customary law shelf are this genre's closest neighbours — and why two manuscripts titled ตำนานพญามังราย, "the tamnan of Phaya Mangrai" (ms 641, Wat Na Pang, Nan; ms 5574, Wat Si Khom Kham), sit in the catalogue under Law rather than here.

Where the tamnan becomes wichaa

The palm-leaf chronicles in this catalogue are title-level records — no transcribed text (see Notes). But the contributed printed treatises do have full text, and one of them shows exactly what the wichaa tradition does with a chronicle. The Supreme Maha Mantra Katha runs a section headed "Great and Valiant Heroes Who Excelled Supremely in Mantras and Incantations" (p.55), and it is pure tamnan, retold as a case record.

Its first hero is พระยาเจือง, Phaya Chueang — the same figure this catalogue holds 10 chronicle witnesses of. The treatise gives him a birth year, a prophecy that he would be a cakravartin, three strategic marriages won by turning up with an elephant-catching expedition, and then the line that matters to a katha book: "supremely skilled in warfare and possessing powerful mantras and great yantras for his protection, [he] could not be touched by any weapon on his body, not even once, even in battle" (p.56). The chronicle is being read as proof that katha and yant work. The treatise even notes the story's spread — "the legend of Thao Hung–Thao Chueang, an epic of the Lao; and the legend of Chao Chueang Han of the Tai Lue of Sipsong Panna."

Its second hero gets four pages and the best scene in the corpus. Nan Thip Chang (pp.57–60): Burmese forces hold Lamphun, Chiang Saen and Chiang Rai; Lampang has no lord, only four officials too busy fighting each other to fight anyone else. Three abbots disrobe to raise a rising and are shot down — the abbot of Wat Na Yang taking a bullet between the eyebrows, his two lieutenants falling as they run to catch him. The victorious Thao Mahayot quarters his army inside Wat Phra That Lampang Luang and taxes the district at spearpoint. A senior monk at Wat Phra Kaeo Chomphu then does the most tamnan thing imaginable: he consults the magical texts to find out who is supposed to save the city, and the texts name a forest hunter, Nan Thip Chang. Thip Chang agrees — but first extracts a public pledge that if he wins, the city is his.

He takes 300 men, arrives at the temple in the dead of night, and goes in alone through the western drainage channel — "which still exists today" — disguised as a courier carrying a letter from Thao Mahayot's own consort. Thao Mahayot is in the Wihan Luang playing chess with his officer and his concubine. Thip Chang hands over the letter, steps back a measured distance, and shoots him dead across the chessboard; the ball passes through and strikes the iron railing around the reliquary, "a mark of which still remains today" (p.60). He leaves by the drain he came in by. The townspeople and the monk crown him with lustral water in 1732, and he founds the dynasty this catalogue holds the chronicle of — ตำนานเจ้าเจ็ดตน, the Seven Lords (ms 4039 and ms 5572 at Wat Si Khom Kham; ms 6599).

Inference — note the two "still remains today" clauses. That is the tamnan's characteristic move: the narrative terminates in a physical mark a reader can go and put a finger on. A drainage channel, a dent in an iron rail, a footprint in rock, a hill where an elephant knelt. The story is not asking to be believed. It is asking to be visited — which is why this genre and the atlas are the same project.

The same treatise section goes on to the love-charm worked by Pu Chao Sa-ming Phrai in the Lilit Phra Lo, a flying betel-quid sent across two hostile muang onto a prince's dais (pp.60–61), and then to the origin-legend behind the ม้าเสพนาง yantra (pp.62–63) — proof that in a wichaa manual, chronicle, literature and ritual instruction are one continuous kind of evidence. The Akhom of Phra Narai does it more briefly, teaching an invisibility mantra as "the mantra the novice monk used when he went down to see the elder Upagutta, who keeps the rains-retreat in the nāga realm" (p.169) — a chronicle-figure cited as the warrant for a working spell.

The shape of the collection

At 1,060 witnesses across 114 named temples, this is the most genuinely pan-Lanna of the large genres. Where the canonical corpus is really one Phrae library, the chronicle spreads: Phrae 259 and Chiang Mai 249 stand almost level, with Phayao (144) and Lampang (118) close behind, then Lamphun (63), Nan (57), Chiang Rai (54), Mae Hong Son (39). Wat Sung Men still leads at temple level with 145 — but that is only 14% of the genre, against its crushing dominance elsewhere; Wat Si Khom Kham holds 88, Wat Mueang Mo 47, Wat Pa Sak Noi 41, Wat Chiang Man — Mangrai's first royal temple in Chiang Mai — 39. Place-counts in this genre carry real regional signal.

Its physical support is canonical: palm-leaf 986 of 1,060 (93%), Tham Lanna 996 (94%), only 40 on mulberry paper. The chronicle was copied for permanence, like the scripture it accompanies, not as a working paper. 684 witnesses carry a date, running from 1574 — ms 4421, a Pathama sampothi at Wat Lai Hin Luang, Lampang — to 2024, ms 6201 at Wat Li, Phayao, which is the most recent witness in the entire archive. A chronicle got recopied for as long as its relic or its muang still mattered, and evidently one still did in 2024.

Language marks the borderland too: alongside 653 Pali and Lan Na and 327 Pali-Northern Thai, there are 32 Shan and 28 Tham Lao witnesses, plus Pali and Shan (20), Pali and Lao (16) and even Pali, Shan and Burmese (10) — the chronicle travelling across the wider Tai Buddhist world. The Sinhalese ancestry is in the shelf itself: 12 copies of the ถูปวงส์ (Thūpavaṃsa, the chronicle of the stupa) and three of the มหาวงส์ (Mahāvaṃsa) sit here, the Ceylon model the Lanna vaṃsa was built on.

Two catalogues wearing one genre

One structural fact governs every count above. This genre is fed by exactly two crawled sources, and they do not overlap in labelling at all: DLNTM supplies all 569 Buddhist Chronicle, all 159 Secular History and the four odd ones out; EFEO supplies all 328 plain Tamnan, and nothing else. The three sub-genres are, in part, two cataloguing houses talking past each other. They do overlap in the field: 20 of EFEO's 44 temples are also DLNTM temples, and at Wat Chiang Man the same bundles are demonstrably catalogued twice — ms 787 and ms 6708 are both the Lamphun great-relic tamnan dated 1833; ms 782 and ms 6703 are both Chae Haeng 1815; ms 790 and ms 6705 are both Chom Yong 1877. Read the Tamnan sub-page before adding any two sub-genre figures together.

Notes

  • Title-level only — this is the crawl priority. Of the 1,060 chronicle witnesses, two have any page records at all: ms 3476 and ms 4361, 29 pages between them. The most narrative genre in the archive currently contains no narrative. Every story on this page is either a title, or comes from a printed treatise, or is marked Tradition holds —. Transcribing even one full Phra Chao Liap Lok would change what this archive can say more than any other single act of work.
  • And both exceptions prove the point. A transcription pass over ms 3476, ตำนานท้าวทั้งสี่, found four DLNTM microfilm contact-sheet frames photographing several palm-leaf strips at once, with body text around 20–25 px of glyph height — below the threshold for reading. What was legible was the annotation layer: a title board reading "๕๖๖. ตำนานท้าวทั้ง ๔ (๑ ผูก) … อ. หางดง จ. เชียงใหม่ … 13 หน้า", one fascicle, seven leaves. The same pass turned up a folder-integrity problem worth knowing about: two of the four frames are a different manuscript, ๓๙๓. ตำนานพระยาธัมมิกราช from Lamphun. Nothing of the storyline — no name or direction of the four lords — is recoverable at this resolution, and none should be cited. Higher-resolution images are the blocker. Ms 4361, meanwhile, is not a chronicle at all: a paper Composition Book school notebook in blue ballpoint, 45 pages, dated by its own colophon to 16–18 January 1973, holding sixteen sections of house-building and life-cycle rite — ปูชาแม่ธรณี, เรียกขวัญ, ท้าวทัง ๔, จักฝังเสาเรือน. It sits in this genre on the strength of the word ตำนาน in one section title.
  • Start with the sixteen. Inference — the Liap Lok witnesses are the highest-value target: one work, 16 copies, seven provinces, 1815–1933. A collation across them would show which stops on the Buddha's itinerary each muang chose to keep — which is a direct measurement of how the north edited its own charter.
  • The relic-chronicles are a gazetteer. Site by site, the that-tamnan are primary sources for the history of the shrine and the polity around it. They should be walked against the wats and the atlas, not just browsed as a list.
  • The chronicle/law seam is real and under-catalogued. Two manuscripts titled Tamnan Phanya Mangrai are filed under Law, not here. Any full Mangrai study has to read across both shelves at once.
  • Watch the sub-genre boundary. The 54/31/15 split of Buddhist Chronicle / Tamnan / Secular History is a labelling artefact as much as a content one. Each sub-page says which parts of its own boundary it does not trust.
